pages.project.spectrogram.selectHarmonic: Hear only harmonic {{harmonic}} of the singer and the take
pages.project.vocal.air.fact.airier: Airier here than usual in this song: the tone is {{db}} dB less clear
pages.project.vocal.air.fact.clearer: Clearer here than usual in this song: the tone is {{db}} dB more focused
pages.project.vocal.air.fact.usual: As clear as usual in this song
pages.project.vocal.air.label: Air
pages.project.vocal.air.look: Air shows as grey haze filling the gaps between the harmonic lines, mostly up high. A clear, focused tone has dark gaps and sharp lines; a breathy one has soft lines in a grey fog.
pages.project.vocal.air.tip.lessAir: Focus the tone here: less air, as if you spoke a little louder and closer. The singer drops the breathiness on this note.
pages.project.vocal.air.tip.moreAir: Let more air into the tone here: sigh into the note and sing it softer and closer, the singer turns breathy on it.
pages.project.vocal.air.title: Air in the voice
pages.project.vocal.air.why: Turning breathy in a verse and full in a chorus is a common way singers colour a song. Each voice is compared with itself across the song, since the microphone, the room and the separation change how much noise there is.
pages.project.vocal.dynamics.fact.fade: Gets softer through the note, about {{db}} dB a second
pages.project.vocal.dynamics.fact.steady: Holds an even level through the note
pages.project.vocal.dynamics.fact.swell: Grows through the note, about {{db}} dB a second
pages.project.vocal.dynamics.label: Dynamics
pages.project.vocal.dynamics.look: Watch how bright the harmonic lines of the long note get from its start to its end: a swell lights more lines higher up as it grows, a fade lets the upper lines go dark first.
pages.project.vocal.dynamics.tip.fade: Let the long note get softer toward its end: start it full and ease the air off as you hold it.
pages.project.vocal.dynamics.tip.steady: Keep the long note even: hold the same air and the same level from start to end, without growing or sagging.
pages.project.vocal.dynamics.tip.swell: Grow through the long note: start it a little softer and give it more air as you hold it, so it swells toward its end.
pages.project.vocal.dynamics.title: Dynamics of the long note
pages.project.vocal.dynamics.why: Shaping a long note, swelling into it or letting it fade, is a large part of the expression of a phrase. Only the shape is compared: loudness itself depends on the microphone and on the mix.
pages.project.vocal.onset.fact.hard: Hits the tone at once: full in {{ms}} ms
pages.project.vocal.onset.fact.leadIn: Breath or a consonant for {{ms}} ms before the tone
pages.project.vocal.onset.fact.scoop: Starts {{semitones}} semitones below and slides up
pages.project.vocal.onset.fact.soft: Swells into the tone over {{ms}} ms
pages.project.vocal.onset.label: Attack
pages.project.vocal.onset.look: A swelling attack fades the harmonic lines in from the left; a hard one starts them with a sharp vertical edge. Grey haze before the lines is breath or a consonant; lines bending up at the start are a scoop.
pages.project.vocal.onset.tip.harder: Start cleaner: have the tone there at once, as on a light, crisp “ah”, with no breathy lead-in or slow fade-in. Don't push.
pages.project.vocal.onset.tip.lessLeadIn: Less air before the tone: get into the vowel about {{ms}} ms sooner.
pages.project.vocal.onset.tip.moreLeadIn: Give the breath or the consonant before the vowel its time: the singer spends about {{ms}} ms on it before the tone starts.
pages.project.vocal.onset.tip.noScoop: Land right on the note: you slide up from below where the singer starts on pitch.
pages.project.vocal.onset.tip.scoop: Start a little under the note and slide up into it: the singer begins about {{semitones}} semitones lower.
pages.project.vocal.onset.tip.softer: Start softer: let the tone grow out of the breath, as if it began with a silent “h”, instead of hitting the note.
pages.project.vocal.onset.title: Attack of the phrase
pages.project.vocal.onset.why: The attack is the first thing heard of a phrase and a large part of a singer's manner.
pages.project.vocal.practice.analyzing: Comparing your try with the singer…
pages.project.vocal.practice.empty: The singer has no place of this kind here.
pages.project.vocal.practice.notSung: You haven't sung this place yet: listen, then try.
pages.project.vocal.practice.title: Practice: {{technique}}
pages.project.vocal.register.fact.belt: Belts: the second harmonic is {{db}} dB louder than the first, the upper ones {{upper}} dB under it
pages.project.vocal.register.fact.full: Full chest-like voice: the first harmonic only {{db}} dB over the second, the upper ones {{upper}} dB under it
pages.project.vocal.register.fact.light: Light head or falsetto voice: the first harmonic {{db}} dB over the second, the upper ones {{upper}} dB under it
pages.project.vocal.register.fact.mixed: Mixed voice: the first harmonic {{db}} dB over the second, the upper ones {{upper}} dB under it
pages.project.vocal.register.label: Register
pages.project.vocal.register.look: Compare the two lowest harmonic lines of the note. In a light head voice or falsetto the lowest line is much brighter than the second and the lines above fade fast; in a full or belted voice the second line is as bright as the first or brighter, and many lines above stay lit.
pages.project.vocal.register.tip.fuller: Stay in a fuller voice here: keep it speech-like and bright, open the vowel a little toward “ah” or “eh”, and don't flip into a light head voice on this note.
pages.project.vocal.register.tip.lighter: Lighten up here: the singer lets this note go into a lighter head voice. Take the weight off, narrow the vowel toward “oo” and let it float instead of pushing.
pages.project.vocal.register.title: Register on the note
pages.project.vocal.register.why: Whether a high note is belted or floated is one of the first things that makes a take sound like or unlike the singer. Judged only from 200 Hz up, where the stem and the microphone keep the lowest harmonic.
pages.project.vocal.release.fact.fall: Drops {{semitones}} semitones at the very end
pages.project.vocal.release.fact.hold: Holds the last note for {{seconds}} s
pages.project.vocal.release.label: Ending
pages.project.vocal.release.look: Follow the harmonic lines of the last note to their end: lines that bend down are a fall, lines that run on are a note held to its full length. The fading grey after the lines is mostly the reverb of the mix, not the singer.
pages.project.vocal.release.tip.fall: Let the end fall: relax and slide down about {{semitones}} semitones as the tone goes, the singer drops off the note.
pages.project.vocal.release.tip.longer: Hold the last note longer: the singer keeps it for {{seconds}} s, you for {{yours}} s. Keep the air going to the very end of the phrase.
pages.project.vocal.release.tip.noFall: Hold the pitch to the end: you slide down off the note where the singer stays on it.
pages.project.vocal.release.tip.shorter: End the last note sooner: the singer lets it go after {{seconds}} s, you hold it for {{yours}} s.
pages.project.vocal.release.title: Ending of the phrase
pages.project.vocal.release.why: Falls at the end of a phrase are among the most frequent pop techniques, and how long the last note is held shapes the phrasing.
pages.project.vocal.timing.fact.early_on: Your vowel starts {{ms}} ms before the singer's
pages.project.vocal.timing.fact.early_ot: Your vowels start {{ms}} ms before the singer's, over {{count}} vowels of the phrase
pages.project.vocal.timing.fact.late_one: Your vowel starts {{ms}} ms after the singer's
pages.project.vocal.timing.fact.late_oth: Your vowels start {{ms}} ms after the singer's, over {{count}} vowels of the phrase
pages.project.vocal.timing.fact.overall: The whole take sits {{ms}} ms off the singer; that part is left to the latency calibration and not counted here
pages.project.vocal.timing.fact.singer: The vowels land where the singer puts them
pages.project.vocal.timing.label: Timing
pages.project.vocal.timing.look: Each vowel starts where its harmonic lines light up after a consonant or a pause. Compare where the lines start on your band with the singer's band right under it.
pages.project.vocal.timing.tip.earlier: Come in earlier in this phrase: your vowels land about {{ms}} ms late. Put the consonant before the beat so the vowel itself is on it.
pages.project.vocal.timing.tip.later: Hold back in this phrase: your vowels land about {{ms}} ms early. Wait for the beat and let the vowel start on it.
pages.project.vocal.timing.title: Timing of the vowels
pages.project.vocal.timing.why: Listeners hear the beat of a syllable at the start of its vowel, so a phrase that is steadily early or late sounds rushed or dragging even when every note is right.
pages.project.vocal.transition.fact.over: Overshoots the new note by {{cents}} cents and settles back
pages.project.vocal.transition.fact.slid: Slides {{semitones}} semitones to the next note over {{ms}} ms
pages.project.vocal.transition.fact.step: Steps {{semitones}} semitones to the next note in {{ms}} ms
pages.project.vocal.transition.label: Transition
pages.project.vocal.transition.look: Between two notes the harmonic lines either jump at once, bend smoothly from one height to the other, or swing past the new note and come back. The bend is clearest on the upper lines, where it is many times wider.
pages.project.vocal.transition.tip.noOve: Land on the new note without swinging past it: aim at the note itself and arrive gently.
pages.project.vocal.transition.tip.overs: Swing a little past the new note, about {{cents}} cents, and settle back onto it, as if the voice ran over the step.
pages.project.vocal.transition.tip.slide: Connect the notes with a slide: keep the tone going and glide to the next note over about {{ms}} ms instead of jumping.
pages.project.vocal.transition.tip.step: Step cleanly: the singer jumps to the next note at once, without the glide you put between them.
pages.project.vocal.transition.title: Transition between notes
pages.project.vocal.transition.why: How a singer gets from note to note, with slides, bends and overshoots, is one of the clearest marks of a style and it carries over to any song.
pages.project.vocal.versions.title: Hear yourself with the singer's
pages.project.vocal.vibrato.fact.vibrato: Vibrato from {{delay}} s into the note, {{rate}} waves a second, ±{{cents}} cents
pages.project.vocal.vibrato.label: Vibrato
pages.project.vocal.vibrato.look: Vibrato shows as wavy harmonic lines. The wave grows with the harmonic number, so it is easiest to see high up: see where on the note the waves begin, how dense and how deep they are.
pages.project.vocal.vibrato.tip.add: Add vibrato: hold the note straight for {{delay}} s, then let it waver about {{rate}} times a second, ±{{cents}} cents, relaxed and carried by the breath, not shaken by the jaw.
pages.project.vocal.vibrato.tip.earlier: Let the vibrato in sooner: the singer starts it about {{delay}} s into the note.
pages.project.vocal.vibrato.tip.faster: A faster vibrato: the singer has about {{rate}} waves a second, you {{yours}}. The speed changes slowly with practice, the start and the width matter more.
pages.project.vocal.vibrato.tip.later: Start the vibrato later: hold the note straight for {{delay}} s first, then let it spin.
pages.project.vocal.vibrato.tip.narrower: A narrower vibrato: the singer swings ±{{cents}} cents, you ±{{yours}}. Lighten up and push less.
pages.project.vocal.vibrato.tip.slower: A slower vibrato: the singer has about {{rate}} waves a second, you {{yours}}. The speed changes slowly with practice, the start and the width matter more.
pages.project.vocal.vibrato.tip.straight: Hold it straight: the singer keeps this note without vibrato. Keep the air steady and don't let the tone waver.
pages.project.vocal.vibrato.tip.wider: A wider vibrato: the singer swings ±{{cents}} cents, you ±{{yours}}. Let the tone move more freely.
pages.project.vocal.vibrato.title: Vibrato on the note
pages.project.vocal.vibrato.why: Where vibrato starts, how wide it is and on which notes it appears are among the most recognisable traits of a singer.
pages.project.vocal.vowel.fact.close: A more closed vowel than usual: {{db}} dB less energy from 600 Hz to 1 kHz
pages.project.vocal.vowel.fact.front: A brighter, more forward vowel than usual: {{db}} dB more energy from 1.6 to 2.5 kHz
pages.project.vocal.vowel.fact.open: A more open vowel than usual: {{db}} dB more energy from 600 Hz to 1 kHz
pages.project.vocal.vowel.fact.round: A rounder, darker vowel than usual: {{db}} dB less energy from 1.6 to 2.5 kHz
pages.project.vocal.vowel.label: Vowel
pages.project.vocal.vowel.look: A vowel shows as two bright zones among the harmonic lines: the first zone sits higher the more open the mouth, the second sits higher the more forward the tongue. Compare where the brightest lines of the note sit on your band and on the singer's.
pages.project.vocal.vowel.tip.close: Narrow the vowel here: drop the jaw less, the singer keeps this vowel more closed.
pages.project.vocal.vowel.tip.front: Brighten the vowel here: bring the tongue forward and smile a little, the singer's vowel sits more forward.
pages.project.vocal.vowel.tip.open: Open the vowel here: drop the jaw a little more, the singer sings this vowel more open.
pages.project.vocal.vowel.tip.round: Round the vowel here: bring the lips forward a little, the singer's vowel is darker and rounder.
pages.project.vocal.vowel.title: Vowel colour
pages.project.vocal.vowel.why: The shape of a vowel colours the voice more than anything else. A prototype: only notes up to 350 Hz, where the harmonics are dense enough to show the vowel, and each voice is compared with its own average vowel.
